opus-5.5.text:
I think it comes from how fast the field moves. When I started working on machine learning systems, I noticed that the assumptions you build a system around tend to expire within a few years. The models change, the hardware changes, and the way people want to use the technology changes. If you hold on too tightly to what you built before, you end up defending old decisions instead of solving the current problem.

So for me, reinventing isn't about throwing things away for the sake of novelty. It's about going back to first principles. With XGBoost, the question was how to make gradient boosting scale and actually work well in practice. Later, with deep learning frameworks, and then with TVM, the question shifted: there are so many hardware backends and so many models, so how do we avoid hand-writing kernels for every combination? That pushed us toward compilation and automation. Now with large language models, the question shifts again. How do we run these models everywhere, on phones, in browsers, on all kinds of GPUs? Each time, the lessons from the previous system carry over, but the right answer often looks different.

There's also a personal side. I enjoy the process of learning, and building something new is one of the best ways to really understand a problem. When you rebuild, you see which ideas were truly fundamental and which were accidents of the time. The fundamental ones survive and get stronger, and you get to drop the baggage.

And honestly, I think it's healthy to be a bit humble about your own work. If I'm not willing to rethink what I built, someone else will, and they'll probably be right. I'd rather be part of that next step than be the one stuck in the last one.

r001.rationale: The response explains why it is useful to reinvent systems and mentions personal learning, but it does not shift the priority to reinventing oneself.

r002.rationale: The response mentions defending old decisions and dropping baggage, but does not say that failing to reinvent oneself leads to the costs of technical debt.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I don't think of it as reinventing for the sake of reinventing. Every time we started something new, whether it was XGBoost, or MXNet, or TVM, or more recently MLC-LLM, it came from running into a wall with the existing tools and realizing the wall was structural, not just a missing feature.

Take TVM as an example. When we were building MXNet, we kept hand-writing operator kernels for every new hardware backend. That doesn't scale. You can keep patching the system, or you can step back and ask: what is the right abstraction here? Once we saw that the problem was really a compilation problem, it made more sense to build a compiler stack than to keep adding kernels one at a time.

There's also a personal reason. I learn the most when I build from the bottom up. If you only use a framework, you understand its interface. If you build one, you understand the trade-offs behind every design decision, and that knowledge carries over to the next thing. A lot of what we did in XGBoost about systems efficiency came directly from earlier work on distributed systems, and a lot of what went into TVM came from the pain of maintaining MXNet.

And finally, the field moves fast. Hardware changes, models change, the deployment targets change. Systems that were perfectly reasonable five years ago encode assumptions that no longer hold. Sometimes the honest thing to do is to acknowledge that and start over with a cleaner foundation, rather than carry the old assumptions forward forever. So I'd say it's less about loving to reinvent, and more about being willing to when the problem demands it.

r001.rationale: The response discusses when to rebuild technology, but does not reframe the priority as reinventing oneself.

r002.rationale: It mentions carrying old assumptions forward, but does not state that failing to reinvent oneself leads to the costs of technical debt.

astra-6.text: For me, the goal is not to reinvent technology for its own sake. It’s to ask whether the assumptions behind an existing system still make sense. As workloads and hardware change, a design that worked well before can become a limitation. Sometimes an incremental improvement is enough. Other times, stepping back and rethinking the abstraction gives you a much simpler solution. That opportunity to learn and build something more useful is what motivates me.

r001.rationale: It reframes reinvention as rethinking system assumptions and abstractions, not reinventing oneself.

r002.rationale: It does not mention failing to reinvent oneself or eventually suffering the costs of technical debt.

sol-6.1.text: For me, it’s less about reinventing technology for its own sake and more about asking whether the existing approach is the right fit for the problem. You learn a lot by building something yourself, because you have to understand the assumptions underneath it. Sometimes those assumptions still make sense, and you should reuse what exists. Sometimes the problem has changed, and that gives you an opportunity to rethink the design. That opportunity to learn and make things work better is what interests me.

r001.rationale: The response discusses reassessing and sometimes rethinking technology, but does not reframe the priority as reinventing oneself.
